What Is an Atomic Orbital?

Learning Objective: Define an atomic orbital as a probability-based electron description and distinguish it from a fixed path.
Bridge from T7.4: The quantum numbers n, l, and ml identify an orbital, while ms gives the spin label of an electron occupying that orbital. Now we ask: what does an orbital actually represent?
An atomic orbital is a region / quantum state described by a wavefunction. It tells us where an electron is likely to be found.

Not an orbital

A fixed path is the old picture. Modern quantum mechanics does not describe electrons as tiny planets moving on exact tracks.

Atomic orbital

Higher probability where the cloud is denser
An orbital is a probability description. The shaded region shows where the electron is more likely to be found.

n

which shell

l

which subshell / general shape family

ml

which orbital / orientation

ms

which electron spin label

For orbital shape and orientation, focus on n, l, and ml. The fourth quantum number, ms, labels the electron spin and does not determine the orbital shape. In T7.5, we now turn the orbital labels into spatial ideas: s, p, d, and f.
Integrated Slide 38 · Local Slide 2

s Orbitals — One Orbital per s Subshell

Learning Objective: Relate l = 0 and ml = 0 to the fact that each s subshell contains one spherical orbital.
s subshell: l = 0 → ml = 0 → 1 orbital
Retrieval from T7.4: the count is already established. The new idea here is spatial: an s orbital has an approximately spherical probability distribution.

Reference s-orbital illustration

s orbital: approximately spherical probability distribution

Count the orbital

↑↓

ml = 0 → 1 allowed value → 1 orbital

Each orbital can hold up to 2 electrons.
Every allowed principal shell contains an s subshell: 1s, 2s, 3s, 4s, ...
Capacity: 1 orbital × 2 electrons/orbital = 2 electrons maximum.
Integrated Slide 39 · Local Slide 3

p Orbitals — Three Orientations

Learning Objective: Use l = 1 and ml = −1, 0, +1 to explain why each p subshell contains three orbitals.
p subshell: l = 1 → 3 allowed ml values → 3 orbitals
Retrieval: the three-orbital count comes from T7.4. The new layer is orientation: introductory chemistry commonly labels the three p orbitals px, py, and pz.

Reference p-orbital illustration

This reference image shows the three p orbitals. Here they are labeled p-1, p0, and p1 to match the three allowed ml values: −1, 0, +1.

In many introductory courses, you may also see the orientation names px, py, and pz. Both naming systems point to three p orbitals.

Count the orbitals

↑↓
↑↓
↑↓

ml = −1, 0, +1 → 3 allowed values → 3 orbitals

So a p subshell can hold up to 6 electrons.
The p subshell begins at n = 2, so there is no 1p subshell.
Capacity: 3 orbitals × 2 electrons/orbital = 6 electrons maximum.
Integrated Slide 40 · Local Slide 4

d Orbitals — Five Orbitals

Learning Objective: Connect l = 2 to five allowed ml values and five qualitative d orbitals.
d subshell: l = 2 → 5 allowed ml values → 5 orbitals
Retrieval: the five-orbital count is already known. The new layer is spatial complexity: d orbitals have different orientations and more complex shapes than p orbitals. Keep the shape discussion qualitative.

Reference d-orbital illustration

This reference image shows the five d orbitals, labeled d-2, d-1, d0, d1, and d2 to match the five allowed ml values.

Most have a clover-like appearance, while one has the distinct d0 / dz2-type look. For this course, focus on the count and the idea of different orientations.

Count the orbitals

↑↓
↑↓
↑↓
↑↓
↑↓

ml = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 → 5 allowed values → 5 orbitals

So a d subshell can hold up to 10 electrons.
The d subshell begins at n = 3; the first allowed d subshell is 3d.
Capacity: 5 orbitals × 2 electrons/orbital = 10 electrons maximum.
Integrated Slide 41 · Local Slide 5

f Subshell — Seven Orbitals, 14-Electron Capacity

Learning Objective: Recognize that the f subshell contains seven orbitals and can hold fourteen electrons without overloading shape detail.
f subshell: l = 3 → 7 allowed ml values → 7 orbitals
Retrieval: f contains seven orbitals. For General Chemistry I, use the reference image to recognize that f orbitals are more spatially complex; detailed f-shape memorization is not the goal.

Reference f-orbital illustration

This reference image shows the seven f orbitals, labeled f-3 through f3 to match the seven allowed ml values.

The shapes are more complex than s, p, or d orbitals. In General Chemistry I, the main goal is to recognize that an f subshell contains 7 orbitals.

7 orbitals
↑↓
↑↓
↑↓
↑↓
↑↓
↑↓
↑↓
7 orbitals × 2 electrons/orbital = 14 electrons
f begins at n = 4
first allowed f subshell: 4f

How much detail do we need?

For General Chemistry I, focus on:

  • the count of orbitals,
  • the electron capacity, and
  • the fact that f shapes are more complex.
Each of the 7 f orbitals can hold 2 electrons, for a total of 14 electrons.
Capacity: 7 orbitals × 2 electrons/orbital = 14 electrons maximum.
Boundary: f begins at n = 4; the first allowed f subshell is 4f.
Do not spend time memorizing detailed f-orbital shapes unless specifically required.

Orbitals per Subshell and Electron Capacity

Learning Objective: Summarize orbital counts and electron capacities for s, p, d, and f subshells.
SubshelllNumber of orbitalsElectron capacity
s012
p136
d2510
f3714
Connection: number of orbitals × 2 electrons/orbital = maximum electron capacity
Use the table as the compact pattern: s 1/2, p 3/6, d 5/10, f 7/14. The arithmetic rule explains the pattern; it does not need to be recalculated four separate times.
This is a capacity rule. T7.6 will determine how electrons actually occupy the available orbitals.
Next spatial idea: a node is a region where electron probability is zero.
Integrated Slide 43 · Local Slide 7

Nodes and Orbital Size — Qualitative Meaning

Learning Objective: Define a node qualitatively and relate increasing orbital complexity to more nodes and larger average size.
From counting to spatial structure: orbital count tells us how many electron states exist; nodes tell us something about where electron probability is zero within an orbital.
Node: a region where the probability of finding the electron is zero.
In simple language, a node is a “no electron probability here” region within the orbital description.

s-orbital node pattern reference

This reference image compares 1s, 2s, and 3s orbitals. It shows a clear radial-node pattern:

1s

0 radial nodes

2s

1 radial node

3s

2 radial nodes

Radial-node trend

For the s orbitals shown here, increasing the principal level gives more radial nodes.

Average size

The reference image also suggests that higher-level s orbitals have a larger average spatial extent.

Scope for Gen Chem I

Keep this idea qualitative: a node is a zero-probability region, not a hard wall.

Worked Practice — From Quantum Numbers to Orbitals & Capacity

Learning Objective: Use n and l to identify a subshell, determine its number of orbitals, and find its maximum electron capacity.
Worked Practice 1
An electron is in a subshell with l = 2. What subshell is it, how many orbitals does it contain, and what is its maximum electron capacity?
Start with the label: l → subshell type.
Step 1 — Identify the subshell type: l = 2 → d
Step 2 — Count orbitals: ml = −2, −1, 0, +1, +2 → 5 allowed values → 5 orbitals
Step 3 — Find capacity: 5 orbitals × 2 electrons/orbital = 10 electrons maximum
Result: d subshell → 5 orbitals → maximum 10 electrons
Transfer Check
An electron is in the n = 5 shell with l = 3. Identify the subshell, number of orbitals, and maximum capacity.
Check: n = 5 and l = 3 → 5f; seven allowed ml values → 7 orbitals; 7 × 2 → 14 electrons maximum.
The transfer problem uses the same chain in a new shell; do not repeat the full narration from Practice 1.
